subject: Business Models
title: Timing Beats Everything
description: Learn Timing Beats Everything in one minute.

hook.text: Webvan was 2-decade-early Instacart. Friendster was early Facebook. Timing is the #1 predictor of startup success.

buildup.text: Bill Gross studied 200 companies and found that timing accounted for 42% of the difference between success and failure.

discovery.text: Too early: infrastructure and customers aren't ready. Too late: markets are saturated with competitors.

twist.text: YouTube launched in 2005 when broadband adoption hit 50%. The same idea in 2000 (broadband at 5%) would have failed.

climax.text: The right idea at the wrong time is still the wrong idea. Timing isn't luck—it's reading market readiness correctly.

punchline.text: 42% of success is timing. The right idea at the wrong time still fails.

quiz.question: According to Bill Gross's research, what is the top factor in startup success?

details.summary: Market timing is the most important factor in startup success, more significant than team, product, or funding. Too early means burning cash educating an unready market. Too late means fighting entrenched competitors..
details.whyItMatters: Webvan failed in 2001 with grocery delivery but Instacart succeeded a decade later. A study of over 200 startups found that timing accounted for 42 percent of the difference between success and failure, more than any other single factor.
takeaways: Timing is the single most important factor in startup success or failure
Being too early costs as much as being too late to a maturing market
Webvan failed in 2001 with the same model Instacart profited from in 2012

faq.question: Why is being too early just as bad as being too late?
faq.answer: Being too early means spending capital educating a market that is not ready, building infrastructure before demand exists, and running out of money before customers arrive. The company bears all the pioneering costs while later entrants benefit from the market it helped create.

faq.question: How can founders evaluate whether the timing is right?
faq.answer: Look for enabling technologies reaching critical adoption, shifting consumer behaviors creating demand, regulatory changes opening markets, and adjacent market successes validating related business models. The ideal moment is when infrastructure exists but incumbents have not yet adapted.
